units.title: Established alternative L1s
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

code.title: producer branch coverage
code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 23 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. If an endpoint refuses your client (HTTP 403, 429 or a challenge page), record that and use another public endpoint; do not try to get around the refusal and use no API keys. Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Leads L-1030 and L-1040. Cycle 23 replayed 163,758 mined PoolManager transactions on ten networks word by word against a model of src/ and found no difference (research/network-risk/cycles/023/theme-state-replay.work, scripts/model.py, scripts/run.py, per network results in results/<chainId>/result.json and the traces under raw/<chainId>/tx on this machine). Its own mutation test shows the limit of that result: a wrong tick bitmap bit shows up in 1 to 5 of 300 transactions and a rounding change in getAmount0Delta in 28 to 58. So zero mismatches says little about TickBitmap and the round-up branches, and nobody has listed which branch sides of the PoolManager the block producers of MegaETH (closed JIT executor, finding F-118), Monad (compiled code, F-130) and HyperEVM (closed validator, F-120) have ever executed. A fault on a branch side that no mined transaction has taken would be untested on the code that writes blocks. Task 1: for MegaETH, Monad and HyperEVM, run the PoolManager frames of the replayed transactions through research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py from their recorded prestate (or re-fetch the prestate where it is missing) and record for every conditional jump in research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json how often each side was taken. Since storage, logs and return data of these transactions equal the model, the producer took the same path. Report per network: jumps taken both ways, one way only, never. Task 2: report the same for these arithmetic sites, with the operand ranges seen: the prod1 != 0 branch of FullMath.mulDiv and the MULMOD and remainder subtraction behind it, the round-up increment of mulDivRoundingUp, both rounding branches of SqrtPriceMath.getNextSqrtPriceFromAmount0RoundingUp and getNextSqrtPriceFromAmount1RoundingDown, getAmount0Delta and getAmount1Delta with roundUp, TickMath.getTickAtSqrtPrice and getSqrtPriceAtTick within 2^16 of the bounds and at negative ticks (SAR and SIGNEXTEND paths), TickBitmap.nextInitializedTickWithinOneWord at word boundaries and for negative compressed ticks (the SAR, SHL, BYTE and bit scan sites), LiquidityMath.addDelta with a negative delta, the int128 and int256 casts of BalanceDelta, and the fee arithmetic of Pool.swap with a protocol fee. Task 3: for each site or branch side the producer has never executed on one of the three networks, say whether an ordinary account can reach it, with which call, and whether funds depend on its result. Then look for mined evidence of that site on that network outside the replay window (logs of the pools that would take it, for example swaps that cross a word boundary at negative ticks or exact output swaps that end at a price limit), fetch those transactions and replay them with scripts/model.py. Task 4 (L-1040): on Base, Monad and MegaETH select from the replayed transactions those that flip a bitmap bit, cross a bitmap word boundary or take a round-up branch in SqrtPriceMath, rerun scripts/mutate.py on that subset only, and report the detection rate per mutation. State plainly which sites stay untested on a producer after this.

The cycle 23 replay windows (research/network-risk/cycles/023/theme-state-replay.work, results/<chainId>/result.json, scripts/collect.py, scripts/model.py) were built from PoolManager logs, so every replayed transaction succeeded and carried a log. Two kinds of mined transaction were never compared with the source. A producer that wrongly reverts a burn, a take or a modifyLiquidity freezes funds without leaving a wrong word anywhere, and a transaction that only settles or takes native value, clears a delta, syncs, or collects protocol fees writes no PoolManager log. Task 1 (L-1036): on the ten networks of that replay, over the same block windows, list mined transactions with receipt status 0 that entered the PoolManager (from trace_filter, debug_traceBlockByNumber with callTracer, or block bodies filtered by the known router and position manager addresses). Replay each from the parent state with the model and compare the reverting frame, the revert data and the gas-independent cause. Classify every revert as a source revert with its custom error, an out-of-gas, or something the source does not explain. Anything in the third class is the result to report in full. Task 2 (L-1035): cycle 23 counted 3,135 of 20,000 MegaETH transactions with a PoolManager frame that reverted and was caught, against 2 to 165 on the other networks. Group those frames by revert data and by the program counter where the revert started. Say whether any comes from a MegaETH resource limit (compute gas, KV update, data size or state growth in mega-evm limit.rs at the tag the endpoint reports) and not from a revert in src/, and whether such a limit can stop a frame after take has paid out and before settle, in a way that leaves the outer transaction successful. Task 3 (L-1025): find mined PoolManager transactions without a PoolManager log on Ethereum, Base, Monad, MegaETH and HyperEVM (call traces of blocks in the window, selectors settle, settleFor, take, clear, sync, mint, burn, collectProtocolFees, updateDynamicLPFee, setProtocolFee) and replay them word by word as cycle 23 did, including the native balance. Task 4: for the reverts the model predicts, check the opposite direction on a sample of 2,000 successful transactions per network: does the model predict success for each (it should, they are in the replay), and for 200 mined failed transactions per network, does an eth_call of the same call at the parent block on a second endpoint with a different client build revert the same way.

Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Lead L-1034. Avalanche folds storage slot S and S with bit 248 flipped into one entry (finding F-040), a client rule that sits between SSTORE and the state store and that no opcode test at a single slot can see. The PoolManager derives every pool, tick, bitmap, position and ERC-6909 slot with KECCAK256 and reads and writes them with SLOAD, SSTORE, TLOAD and TSTORE (src/libraries/Pool.sol, src/libraries/StateLibrary.sol for the layout, src/libraries/Lock.sol, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol, CurrencyReserves.sol and CurrencyDelta.sol for the transient slots). This theme asks whether any other client on the 21 networks transforms, buckets, truncates or caches keys or hashes on that path. Task 1: read, at the release each endpoint reports today, how these clients turn (address, slot) into a state store key and how their caches key entries: mega-evm and the MegaETH stateless validator (SALT bucket mapping, the witness format), Monad v0.16.5 and v0.16.7 (category/execution/ethereum/db, TrieDb key encoding, the state and version caches of parallel execution), nanoreth nb-20261125-2 (state patches, precompile and system account handling), coreth or the Avalanche EVM at the reported commit and Firewood if enabled (the F-040 rule itself and any second rule like it), bor v2.11.x (PBSS, the block STM multi-version store keys, the widened keccak cache and the MULMOD memo), bsc v1.8.2 and reth-bsc, Nitro v3.13.0 (ArbOS storage-backed state under its own account, Stylus caches), reth and op-reth at the reported versions, Tempo and Arc (precompile storage under fixed addresses), celo-reth and X Layer. For each, quote the lines and answer three questions: can two different (address, slot) pairs share one entry; can a persistent and a transient slot share one entry; is any cache keyed by something narrower than the full key (a truncated hash, a pointer, a per-transaction index that is reused) and if so what happens on a collision. Task 2: do the same for caches in front of KECCAK256 (any memo of hash results keyed by input, length or memory pointer), since a stale hash would send a pool write to the wrong slot. Task 3: for every rule or cache found, say whether an ordinary account can choose a slot, an address (CREATE2 salt mining) or an input so that its own write lands on, or its read returns, a PoolManager entry, and how many bits it would have to match. Task 4: test what can be tested without transactions: with eth_call state overrides at the real PoolManager address on each network, write pairs of slots that the rule would fold (for F-040 the bit 248 pair, for others whatever task 1 found) and read them back through extsload (src/Extsload.sol) and exttload; for the transient case set a persistent slot by override and read the same index with exttload after a TSTORE of another value in the same call. Record every pair that reads back differently from Ethereum.

Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Leads L-1031, L-1026, L-1017 and L-1041. The HyperEVM validator is closed and its headers carry no usable state root (finding F-120). Cycle 23 showed that the official endpoint rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm and two nanoreth replicas hold the same latest word in all 8,464 PoolManager slots ever written, and that 2,833 mined transactions replay to the source on a replica (research/network-risk/cycles/023/theme-hyperevm-twin-state.work and research/network-risk/cycles/023/theme-state-replay.work, results/999). Two things are still unknown. First, whether eth_call on the official endpoint runs in the EVM that produces blocks: the 185,529 vector battery and the script sets on HyperEVM count as evidence about the validator only if it does. Second, whether the validator wrote the same words as the replica block by block, since a latest-state comparison sees only the last write of each word. Task 1 (L-1031): build a short probe set whose answers differ between EVM implementations in ways that are not arithmetic and are documented or visible in public source: the error text of a stack underflow, an invalid jump and an out-of-gas in eth_call, the gas left reported by GAS after a cold and a warm SLOAD and after a CALL to an empty account, the return data and gas use of a failed precompile call (ecrecover with bad v, modexp with huge lengths, the 0x0a point evaluation with a bad proof), eth_estimateGas for a call that reverts at exactly one gas value, the handling of a state override with stateDiff against state, and eth_call with a block hash. Run it on the official endpoint, on both nanoreth replicas and on a go-ethereum and a reth mainnet endpoint for reference, and say which family the official endpoint answers like. Read the Hyperliquid documentation and the nanoreth README for what they say about how hl-node executes and how the official RPC is served. Task 2 (L-1026): the official endpoint ignores the block argument, so sample it over time: poll the latest value of every PoolManager word that recent transactions touch (take the hot pools from the newest logs), stamp each read with eth_blockNumber before and after, and compare with the replica's value at the same block. Run this over as many blocks with PoolManager activity as the cycle allows and report words compared and differences. Task 3 (L-1017): repeat the 8,464 slot comparison with the bitmap words between each recent swap's start and end tick added, and extend the gas price 0 census past the 5,405 blocks of cycle 23. Task 4 (L-1041, for finding F-020): from the Hyperliquid API reference and the aligned quote asset documentation, does HyperCore accept an address with EVM code, in particular a contract it did not deploy, as the AQAv2 treasury address of a token, and is there any path other than the staked deployer's action plus a validator vote that sets it. Report what an ordinary account can and cannot do in each task.
